THE Scottish Greens are set to vote on whether to support new nuclear power at their upcoming party conference. If passed, the policy change would leave the SNP as the only party in Holyrood to oppose the development of new nuclear power stations in Scotland.
The Greens will meet in Inverness this weekend for their autumn conference, where they will debate a motion supporting the construction of new nuclear plants provided certain conditions are met.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Proposals for an energy park in north Caithness featuring up to five wind turbines have been condemned as “a new low point in the treatment of rural residents”.
Koehler Renewable Energy (KRE) UK has submitted plans to the Scottish Government’s Energy Consents Unit for Charleston Energy Park, to the south of the A836 between Barrock and Mey.
If approved, the turbines will have a maximum height of 180 metres and the project will also involve access tracks, grid infrastructure and a battery energy storage system of up to 25MW.
The Save Caithness campaign has warned of “significant landscape and visual impacts on nearby communities” and is calling for objections to be lodged before a deadline of November 9.
Koehler has offered to engage with Save Caithness, saying there is “an emerging myth that wind sector representatives do not want to speak to the public and address their questions and concerns”.
JOHNOGROAT-JOURNAL.CO.UK Caithness energy park plans 'show cavalier disregard for the lives of rural residents'

records.bodyText:
THE battle over the proposed Crosbie Wind Farm has been laid bare in final submissions to a public inquiry, with developers arguing the scheme is vital to Scotland's renewable energy ambitions while objectors claim it would irreversibly damage one of North Ayrshire's scenic areas of undeveloped moorland.
In its closing submission, the applicant Galileo maintained the 14-turbine development complies with national planning policy and should be approved by Scottish Ministers.
The developer argued that evidence presented by its own specialists on noise, planning policy, landscape impacts and renewable energy generation should carry greater weight than objections raised during the inquiry.

On Tuesday, 14 October, the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and DESNZ Permanent Secretary Jonathan Brearley (former Chief Executive of Ofgem) gave oral evidence to Parliament's Energy Select Committee.
The discussion covered familiar arguments: grid bottlenecks are holding back clean power; energy prices remain unacceptably high; the current system is too fragmented; and grid construction must be accelerated through Great British Grid initiative with infrastructure costs shared between consumers, taxpayers and private companies.
The Secretary of State also acknowledged weaknesses in the regulatory framework for network companies.
For SEAS, building faster is not enough. Projects must be necessary, alternatives properly assessed, and value for money demonstrated.
These questions are particularly relevant to Sea Link and LionLink.

records.bodyText:
LionLink: Who pays the price?
SEAS and Walberswick Against LionLink (WALL) are calling on Ofgem to take another look at LionLink's economic case and protect electricity consumers from potentially unnecessary costs.
The figures matter. Ofgem's November 2024 assessment estimated losses to British consumers of £3.1 billion to £6.1 billion over 25 years across three scenarios. Under the cap and floor regime, consumers could ultimately bear the cost if the project underperforms financially.
We're asking for answers:
WALL (Walberswick Against LionLink) is calling for updated economic assessments, greater transparency and a firm 2035 deadline.
SEAS is urging a wider strategic assessment of LionLink alongside Sea Link and other major infrastructure planned for East Suffolk. Better-coordinated offshore infrastructure and shared platforms could help reduce onshore impacts and deliver better value for money.
Supporting renewable energy doesn't mean giving every project a free pass.
Electricity grid investment must be necessary, affordable and in the public interest - with proper scrutiny of the costs, benefits and impacts on our communities.

The Scottish Government has been urged to take a public stake in future offshore projects after ScottishPower's parent company reported profits of more than £2 billion.
Iberdrola, which is based in Bilbao, Spain reported an adjusted net profit of €5.1billion (£4.2bn) for the nine months to September 2026, including €2.7bn (£2.2bn) from its UK operations.
The Our Power campaign is urging the Scottish Government to commit to taking a stake in future renewable energy projects so that more of the nation's renewable wealth benefits Scottish communities.

records.bodyText:
A sincere thank you to Hethersgill Parish Council and residents from across the surrounding communities for welcoming North Carlisle Against Pylons and Substation (NCAPS) to our latest community meeting.
The strength of feeling was unmistakable, with residents and farmers expressing deep concerns about National Grid's proposed Cross Border Connection, the extensive pylon route and the potential North Cumbria mega-substation at Option A.
The meeting brought several important outcomes:
 Growing political recognition: We welcomed David Allen, Labour's mayoral candidate, who made clear his view that Option A was the wrong location for the proposed substation — a statement met with applause. He also committed to working with affected communities and ensuring their concerns are heard should he become Mayor.
 Strengthening the campaign: We outlined the establishment of NCAPS Community Action Limited, providing a formal structure to raise funds, secure specialist legal and technical advice, and mount an evidence-led challenge to the pylon route, its design and the proposed substation location.
 Communities working together: Continued collaboration with the North Cumbria Parish Council Alliance will help ensure communities across the affected area have a coordinated and effective voice.
 Holding Cumberland Council to account: Our petition will be presented to Full Council on 3 November, calling on the Council to take a more proactive role in assessing the cumulative impacts of these proposals and representing affected communities.
It was also encouraging to reflect that representatives from across the mayoral political parties have now engaged with our communities, with concerns about the adequacy of National Grid's consultation extending across party lines.
We are not against upgrading the electricity network. We are challenging how and where that infrastructure is being proposed, and the potentially irreversible consequences for North Cumbria.
More than a year of uncertainty is already taking its toll on residents, farmers and businesses. Continued community engagement, fundraising and support will be essential as NCAPS moves into its next phase.
Thank you again to Hethersgill for hosting us and to everyone who attended, spoke openly and offered their support.
Our greatest strength remains the collective voice of our communities. We need to keep that momentum going.
#NCAPS #NorthCumbria #Hethersgill #CrossBorderConnection #NationalGrid #CommunityVoice #Carlisle

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
THE Scottish Government is facing questions over a minister’s letter which appeared to cast doubt on a commitment to introduce national planning guidance for huge, energyintensive data centres.
Public Finance Minister Hannah Mary Goodlad wrote to Scottish Green MSP Patrick Harvie on October 8 saying ministers were still considering whether to bring forward guidance for hyperscale developments.
However, the letter came just two days after Ms Goodlad confirmed in a written parliamentary answer that the guidance would be published before Christmas. She had also told MSPS in September that the government would bring forward national planning guidance by the end of the year.
